at kaste op.explanation: "At kaste op" means to throw up or vomit. "Kaste" means to throw and "op" means up, so it is the same idea as in English. The word "op" stays at the end: "Han kastede op". Another way to say it is "at brække sig".

sentence.en: The child threw up last night.

forms.en: I have known (a person or place)

at kende.explanation: "At kende" means to know a person, a place or something you are familiar with: "Jeg kender Anna" (I know Anna). To know a fact, use "at vide" instead, as in "Jeg ved, at hun bor her". A simple way to remember it: "kende" is knowing someone, "vide" is knowing something.

sentence.en: I know him well.

at kigge.explanation: "At kigge" means to look or to have a look, and it feels casual and friendly: "Kig her!" (Look here!). It is often used with "på" (at), like "Jeg kigger på billedet". It is a little more relaxed than "at se". In a shop you may hear "Jeg kigger bare", meaning I'm just looking.

sentence.en: I am looking at the picture.

at klemme.explanation: "At klemme" is to squeeze or pinch, for example a lemon or your finger in a door. Its past form is "klemte" (not "klemmede"), which is worth noticing. The noun "en klem" is a squeeze or a hug, and Danes often end informal messages with "kram og klem" (hugs and squeezes).

sentence.da: Pas på, du ikke **klemmer** fingrene i døren.
sentence.en: Be careful you don't pinch your fingers in the door.

at klæde sig på.explanation: "At klæde sig på" means to get dressed. The little word "sig" changes with the person: "jeg klæder mig på", "du klæder dig på", "han klæder sig på". The opposite is "at klæde sig af" (to undress). To put on one item, Danes say "at tage på", such as "at tage en jakke på".

sentence.en: The children are getting dressed.

at koge.explanation: "At koge" means to boil or to cook in boiling water, for example eggs, pasta and potatoes. It can also mean that water is boiling: "Vandet koger". Do not mix it up with "at lave mad", which means to make food in general.

sentence.en: I boil potatoes for dinner.

at komme.explanation: "At komme" means to come, and Danes use it for arriving and for being on the way: "Jeg kommer nu" (I am coming now). "Hvor kommer du fra?" asks where you are from. It is also used for what will happen next, as in "Det kommer til at regne" (It is going to rain). The opposite direction is "at gå".

sentence.en: I come from England.

at komme hjem.explanation: "At komme hjem" means to come home or to arrive home. It focuses on the moment of arriving. A common question is "Hvornår kommer du hjem?" (When do you get home?). For 'have come home' Danish uses "er".

sentence.en: I get home at six o'clock.

at komme ind.explanation: "At komme ind" means to come in or to get in. Use it when someone enters, or when you manage to get inside somewhere. "Kom ind!" is what you say to invite someone in. The opposite is "at komme ud".

sentence.en: You can come in now.

at komme ned.explanation: "At komme ned" means to come down, such as coming down the stairs or from a higher floor. It can also mean getting down from somewhere. The opposite is "at komme op". For 'have come down' Danish uses "er".

sentence.da: Kan du **komme ned** og hjælpe mig?
sentence.en: Can you come down and help me?

forms.en: I have come up / gotten up

at komme op.explanation: "At komme op" means to come up, and also to get up, for example out of bed or up from a chair. In daily talk, "Kom op!" can mean 'Come on!' or 'Get a move on!'. The opposite is "at komme ned".

sentence.en: You must come up to me.

at komme tilbage.explanation: "At komme tilbage" means to come back or to return. "Jeg kommer snart tilbage" means "I will be back soon". The "have" form uses "er": "Jeg er kommet tilbage" (I have come back). The small word "tilbage" always stays after the main word, so it can end up at the end of the sentence.

sentence.en: I will be back soon.

forms.en: I have come out / gotten out

at komme ud.explanation: "At komme ud" means to come out or to get out, of a room, house or building. It is also used when you finally get outside for a while, like "jeg kommer ud i dag". The opposite is "at komme ind". For 'have come out' Danish uses "er".

sentence.en: I get out of the car.

at koste.explanation: "At koste" means to cost. It is mostly used with "det" (it) or "de" (they): "Hvad koster det?" (How much does it cost?), which is one of the most useful shopping questions. It does not describe a person doing something, so the forms start with "det" instead of "jeg".

sentence.en: How much does this blouse cost?

at kunne.explanation: "At kunne" means can or to be able to, so it says what you are able to do or what is possible. It is followed straight by another action word, with no "at" in between: "Jeg kan svømme". The form "kan" is the same for every person. Do not mix it up with "at måtte", which is about permission or need.

sentence.en: I can speak a little Danish.

at kunne lide.explanation: "At kunne lide" means to like, and it is made of three small words: "Jeg kan lide kaffe" (I like coffee). It is a fixed phrase, so the "at" goes in front only once. The word "godt" can be added to make it a bit warmer: "Jeg kan godt lide dig". To say you do not like something, add "ikke": "Jeg kan ikke lide det".

sentence.en: I like coffee.

at købe.explanation: "At købe" means to buy. It is one of the first words you need for shopping: "Jeg vil gerne købe en billet" (I would like to buy a ticket). It is the opposite of "at sælge" (to sell).

sentence.en: I would like to buy a ticket.

at købe ind.explanation: "At købe ind" means to do your shopping, mostly for food and things for the home. "At købe" on its own just means to buy, but "købe ind" is about the weekly shop. You often say "Jeg skal ud og købe ind" (I am going out to shop). The word "ind" here does not mean "in".

sentence.en: I need to buy groceries for dinner.

at køre.explanation: "At køre" means to drive or to ride in a vehicle: "Jeg kører i bil" (I go by car). It is used for anyone who drives, but also for a bus or train that runs. For a bike you usually say "at cykle". A tip: when someone just rides along as a passenger, Danes also say "at køre med".

sentence.en: I drive to work every day.

at køre hjem.explanation: "At køre hjem" means to drive home, in a car or on a bike or bus, anything with wheels. For going on foot, use "at gå hjem". For 'have driven home' Danish uses "er" in this phrase: "jeg er kørt hjem".

sentence.en: I drive home after work.

en kage.explanation: "En kage" is a cake. In Danish it covers many things: birthday cakes, pastries and cookies are often all called "kager". "At bage en kage" is to bake a cake, and "kage" is a big part of Danish coffee and birthday culture.

sentence.da: Vi spiser **kage**, når jeg har fødselsdag.
sentence.en: We eat cake when it is my birthday.

en kalender.explanation: "Kalender" is a calendar, on a wall or in your phone. It is also the thing where you write down appointments, so Danes say "Jeg tjekker min kalender" (I'll check my calendar). The plural is "kalendere".

sentence.en: I look in my calendar.

en kanin.explanation: "En kanin" is a rabbit. Many children keep a rabbit as a pet. A wild rabbit or hare is "en hare", which is a different animal. At Easter you will see "påskeharen" (the Easter bunny), which uses "hare" and not "kanin".

sentence.en: My daughter has a rabbit.

en kartoffel.explanation: "En kartoffel" is a potato, and potatoes are a classic part of Danish dinners. Notice that the "the" form drops an e: "kartoflen". The plural is "kartofler". Danes often shorten it to "kartofler" in talk, as in "kogte kartofler" (boiled potatoes).

sentence.en: We eat potatoes for dinner.

en kasket.explanation: "En kasket" is a cap with a peak at the front, like a baseball cap. It is not the same as "en hue" (a warm knitted beanie) or "en hat" (a hat with a brim). Notice the double t when you add endings: "kasketten", "kasketter". People wear it for the sun or for style.

sentence.en: He is wearing a red cap.

en kat.explanation: "En kat" is a cat. The plural is "katte", with an -e on the end. A kitten is "en killing", and a cat's sound is "mjav". Cats and dogs are the most common pets, so this word comes up a lot in everyday chat.

sentence.en: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

en kiks.explanation: "En kiks" is a biscuit, cracker or cookie. The plural is the same as the single form: "to kiks" (two biscuits). It is not the same as "en kage" (cake), and "en småkage" is the word for a sweet cookie.

sentence.en: I eat a cracker with cheese.

en kilometer.explanation: "En kilometer" is a kilometer, 1,000 meters. Stays the same after a number: "fem kilometer". Distances in Denmark are always in kilometers, and speed is "kilometer i timen" (kilometers per hour). In writing it is "km".

sentence.en: It is three kilometers to the station.

en kind.explanation: "En kind" is the cheek on your face. In Denmark people sometimes greet close friends or family with a kiss or a touch on the cheek, but a handshake is more common with new people. Do not confuse it with the cheeks of your bottom, which have a different word.

sentence.en: She has red cheeks.

en kiosk.explanation: "En kiosk" is a small shop that sells things like drinks, sweets, newspapers and snacks, and it often has long opening hours. You can pop in for a quick small purchase. It is not as big as "et supermarked" (a supermarket). The plural is "kiosker".

sentence.en: I am buying a newspaper at the kiosk.

en kirke.explanation: En kirke is a church. Almost every Danish town and village has an old one, often white with a pointed tower. You say "i kirken" for "in the church". In Danish, "the church" is "kirken". Do not confuse it with "kirkegård", which is a cemetery.

sentence.da: Der er en gammel **kirke** i byen.
sentence.en: There is an old church in the town.

en kjole.explanation: "En kjole" is a dress. Note the "j" in the spelling, which is said roughly like a "y" sound. You can build words from it, such as "en festkjole" for a party dress and "en sommerkjole" for a summer dress.

sentence.en: She is wearing a beautiful dress.

en klasse.explanation: "En klasse" means a school class, the group of pupils, and also the classroom. Danish schools count years as classes: "2. Klasse" is second grade. A classmate is "en klassekammerat".

sentence.da: Der er tyve børn i min **klasse**.
sentence.en: There are twenty children in my class.

en klinik.explanation: "En klinik" is a clinic, a place where you see a doctor or dentist without staying overnight. And the word for more than one doubles the k: "klinikker". A hospital is "et hospital" or "et sygehus", which is bigger.

sentence.en: The clinic opens at eight o'clock.

en kniv.explanation: "En kniv" is a knife. The "k" at the start is pronounced, which is different from English, so say "k-niv". The plural is "knive", without an "r". Be careful with sharp ones: "Den kniv er skarp" (That knife is sharp).

sentence.en: Can I borrow a knife?

en ko.explanation: "En ko" is a cow. Watch the plural: it changes the vowel and becomes "køer" (with an ø), so it is not just "-er" added to ko. You will see cows on every Danish farm, and "mælk" (milk) comes from them.

sentence.en: The cow is standing in the field.

en kok.explanation: "En kok" is a cook or chef, a person who prepares food, often as a job in a restaurant. Do not mix it up with "at koge", which means to boil. The plural is "kokke", and the word is the same for men and women.

sentence.en: The chef makes good food.

en kollega.explanation: "En kollega" is a colleague, someone you work with. Be careful with the plural: it is "kolleger", with the -a dropped. Danish workplaces are fairly informal, so you will often say "mine kolleger" about people you chat with at coffee breaks.

sentence.en: My colleague is called Peter.

en koncert.explanation: "En koncert" is a concert, a live music event. You "går til koncert" (go to a concert) or "hører en koncert". Remember: "the concert" is "koncerten".

sentence.en: We are going to a concert tonight.

en kone.explanation: "En kone" is a wife. It has regular forms. People say "min kone" for my wife. Its pair is "en mand" (a husband). For a woman in general, use "en kvinde", not "kone", which only means a married partner.

sentence.en: My wife works in a bank.

en kop.explanation: "En kop" is a cup. It is typically used for hot drinks: "en kop kaffe" (a cup of coffee) or "en kop te". Do not mix it up with "et glas" (a glass), which is for cold drinks. A small one for coffee is "en kaffekop", which is built from the same word.

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en **kop** kaffe.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of coffee.

en krokodille.explanation: "En krokodille" is a crocodile. It is spelled with a "k" instead of a "c" and has two "l"s, but it sounds a bit like the English word. "Krokodillen" is "the crocodile". You will mostly meet it in the zoo or in children's books and songs.

sentence.en: The crocodile is lying in the river.

en krone.explanation: En krone is a crown, the money used in Denmark. The short form for the price is "kr." and it is said "kroner" when there is more than one: "tyve kroner" is twenty crowns. In Danish, "the crown" is "kronen". One hundredth of a krone is "en øre", but you hardly see coins that small today.

sentence.en: It costs twenty crowns.

en krop.explanation: "En krop" is the body, a person's or an animal's physical self. When Danes say a body part hurts, they usually name the part itself, for example "hovedet" or "maven", and use "kroppen" for general talk like "Kroppen har brug for søvn".

sentence.en: My body is tired after the trip.

en kuffert.explanation: "Kuffert" is a suitcase. You pack it with "at pakke en kuffert" and unpack with "at pakke ud". Danes also use it for a big trunk. Remember the double f and the plural "kufferter".

sentence.en: My suitcase is heavy.

en kuglepen.explanation: "En kuglepen" is a ballpoint pen. It is built from "kugle" (ball) and "pen" (pen), because of the tiny ball at the tip. It is the pen most people use to write and to fill in forms, so it is handy to know at the bank or the doctor.

sentence.en: May I borrow your ballpoint pen?

en kusine.explanation: "En kusine" is a female cousin, the daughter of an aunt or uncle. Danish has separate words for male and female cousins. The male one is "en fætter". The word is spelled with a "k" and an "s", sounding like the French word.

sentence.da: Min **kusine** kommer på besøg i morgen.
sentence.en: My cousin is visiting tomorrow.

en kvinde.explanation: "En kvinde" is the ordinary word for a woman, an adult female person. The opposite is "en mand" (a man), and "en pige" is used for a girl or a young woman.

sentence.da: Den **kvinde** bor ved siden af os.
sentence.en: That woman lives next to us.

en kvittering.explanation: "En kvittering" is a receipt, the paper or message that proves you have paid. You need it if you want to exchange something, so shops often ask "Skal du have kvitteringen?" (Do you want the receipt?). The short everyday word is "en bon", and both are used. It is a longer word, so say it slowly: kvi-te-ring.

sentence.en: Keep the receipt if you want to exchange it.

en kæreste.explanation: "En kæreste" is a boyfriend or girlfriend, a romantic partner you are not necessarily married to. It can be a man or a woman, so it works for anyone. The word comes from "kær" (dear), so it is a warm word. It is used for "my partner" in everyday talk.

sentence.en: My partner is called Emma.

et kilo.explanation: "Et kilo" is short for kilogram and is how Danes talk about weight when shopping. After a number it usually stays the same, so you say "to kilo" (two kilos). Shop signs often write "kr. Pr. Kg" (price per kilo).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have et **kilo** æbler.
sentence.en: I would like a kilo of apples.

et klaver.explanation: "Et klaver" is a piano. Remember: "the piano" is "klaveret". To play it you say "at spille klaver". The word "piano" is also understood, but "klaver" is the normal Danish word.

sentence.da: Hun øver sig på **klaver** hver dag.
sentence.en: She practises the piano every day.

et knæ.explanation: "Et knæ" is a knee. The word for more than one stays the same: "to knæ". The k is pronounced, unlike in English. "Jeg har ondt i knæet" (My knee hurts) is a typical sentence, and you will use it at the doctor's.

sentence.en: My knee hurts.

et kodeord.explanation: "Et kodeord" is a password, literally a "code word". You say "mit kodeord" and "kodeordet" for "the password". The word does not change in the plural: "to kodeord" means two passwords. Danish websites often ask for your "brugernavn og kodeord".

sentence.en: I have forgotten my password.

et kontor.explanation: Et kontor is an office, the room or building where people do desk work. You say "på kontoret" for "at the office". Do not use it for a post office, which is "et posthus". In Danish, "the office" is "kontoret". A person who works there is often just said to "arbejde på et kontor".

sentence.en: She works at the office.

et kort.explanation: "Kort" is a map and also a card, depending on the situation. "Et kort over byen" is a map of the town, and "et kreditkort" is a credit card. The plural looks the same as the single word, so "to kort" means two cards or maps. Also note that "kort" can mean short, so use context.

sentence.en: Do you have a map of the town?

et kæledyr.explanation: "Et kæledyr" is an animal you keep at home for company, such as a dog or a cat. And the word for more than one looks exactly the same: "to kæledyr" (two pets). Farm animals are not kæledyr; they are "husdyr".

sentence.da: Vi har to **kæledyr**: en hund og en kat.
sentence.en: We have two pets: a dog and a cat.

et køkken.explanation: "Et køkken" is a kitchen. The "ø" is a Danish letter, a bit like the vowel in English "bird". It also appears in "at lave mad i køkkenet" (cooking in the kitchen). In a small home people often eat in the kitchen too.

sentence.en: I cook in the kitchen.

et køleskab.explanation: "Køleskab" is the fridge. It is built from "køle" (cool) and "skab" (cupboard), so it is literally a cooling cupboard. You say "i køleskabet" for in the fridge. The freezer is "en fryser".

sentence.en: The milk is in the fridge.

kaffe.explanation: "Kaffe" is coffee, an en-word, so "the coffee" is "kaffen". Danes drink a lot of it, and you will hear "Skal vi have en kop kaffe?" (Shall we have a cup of coffee?) all the time. Note that when you order it you can say "en kaffe, tak" or just "kaffe, tak".

sentence.en: Do you want a cup of coffee?

kakao.explanation: "Kakao" is cocoa, both the powder and the hot chocolate drink. It is an en-word. Danes often order "en varm kakao" in the cold months, and children love it. The word is mostly used on its own for the drink, and there is no everyday plural.

sentence.en: The children drink hot cocoa.

kan du gentage det?.explanation: "Kan du gentage det?" means "Can you repeat that?" and is a polite way to ask someone to say something again. "At gentage" means to repeat. It is useful when someone speaks fast and you did not catch it. You can also say "Kan du sige det igen?" (Can you say it again?) or add "langsommere" (more slowly). Add "tak" to be extra polite.

sentence.en: Sorry, can you repeat that?

kan jeg betale med kort?.explanation: "Kan jeg betale med kort?" means "can I pay by card?". In Denmark almost everywhere takes cards, often even for small things. "Med" means "with", and "kort" is an et-word for card. For cash, say "kan jeg betale kontant?".

sentence.da: **Kan jeg betale med kort?** Jeg har ingen kontanter.
sentence.en: Can I pay by card? I have no cash.

kan jeg købe ...?.explanation: A polite way to ask to buy something in a shop or cafe. "Kan jeg" means "can I", and "købe" is "buy". Put what you want in place of the dots. For a more casual order, Danes often say "jeg vil gerne have.." (I would like..).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **kan jeg købe** en kop kaffe?
sentence.en: Excuse me, can I buy a cup of coffee?

kartofler.explanation: "Kartofler" means potatoes. The single potato is "en kartoffel", and the plural, which you use most, is "kartofler". Potatoes are a main part of traditional Danish dinners, boiled, fried or mashed. A common pattern is "kogte kartofler" (boiled potatoes) with meat and sauce.

sentence.en: We eat potatoes for dinner.

forms.en: I am sorry about it / I am sad about it.

forms.da: Jeg er ked af, at jeg kom for sent.
forms.en: I am sorry that I came too late.

ked af.explanation: "Ked af" means sorry or sad. "Jeg er ked af det" is the standard way to say you are sorry and also that you feel sad. Add "at" and a sentence to say why: "ked af, at jeg kom for sent". It is softer than "undskyld", which is a quick "excuse me".

sentence.en: I am sorry about that.

ked af det.explanation: "Ked af det" means sad or upset, and it is always used as a fixed phrase after "er" (am, is, are): "Jeg er ked af det." It is not the same as "ked af", which also means sorry: "Jeg er ked af det" can mean both "I am sad" and "I am sorry", and context tells you which. The opposite is "glad" (happy). In writing, keep all three words together.

sentence.en: Why are you sad?

kedelig.explanation: "Kedelig" means boring, for things and people. It can also mean unfortunate or a pity: "Det er kedeligt" often means "That is too bad". Add "t" for et-words ("et kedeligt møde") and "-e" for more than one. If you are bored yourself, say "Jeg keder mig" (I am bored). The opposite is "interessant" or "sjov".

sentence.en: The film was very boring.

ketchup.explanation: "Ketchup" is ketchup, the red tomato sauce, and it is an en-word. With "the" the "p" is doubled: "ketchuppen". It is not counted, so you say "noget ketchup". The English spelling is the same.

sentence.da: Vil du have **ketchup** til pommes frites?
sentence.en: Do you want ketchup with the fries?

kina.explanation: "Kina" is China. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Kina" means "in China" and "til Kina" means "to China". A person is "en kineser" and the language is "kinesisk". The word is spelled with a K in Danish, not a C.

sentence.en: I would like to see China.

kinesisk.explanation: "Kinesisk" means Chinese, for the language and for things from China. It is written with a small letter. It stays the same before an et-word, because it already ends in -sk. "Kinesisk mad" is Chinese food.

sentence.en: I am learning Chinese at evening school.

klar.explanation: "Klar" means ready or clear. "Er du klar?" means "Are you ready?" and "Det er klart" means "Of course" or "That is clear". It is also used for clear weather, water and sky. Add "t" for et-words ("et klart svar") and "-e" for more than one. The word "færdig" is also related, but it means finished, not ready.

sentence.en: Are you ready to go?

klokken.explanation: "Klokken" is used for telling the time. "Hvad er klokken?" means What time is it?, and "Klokken er tre" means It is three o'clock. It is literally "the clock". Use it to say at what time something happens too: "Vi mødes klokken otte". In writing, "kl." is a short form.

sentence.en: It is eight o'clock in the morning.

klokken er fem.explanation: This is how to tell the time on the hour: "klokken er" plus the number. Danes use the 24-hour clock in writing and on schedules, so 17:00 is "klokken er sytten" there, but in speech "fem" is common. The word "klokken" is often left out in short answers: just "fem".

sentence.da: **Klokken er fem**, og jeg skal hjem.
sentence.en: It's five o'clock, and I have to go home.

kogt.explanation: "Kogt" means boiled or cooked in water. It comes from the verb "at koge" and gets an extra -e before plural words, like "kogte æg". It is common in food talk: "kogte kartofler" and "et kogt æg". The opposite in meaning is "rå" (raw), and a fried egg is "et stegt æg".

sentence.da: Jeg spiser et **kogt** æg til morgenmad.
sentence.en: I eat a boiled egg for breakfast.

kold.explanation: "Kold" means cold, for weather, drinks, food and also people who seem unfriendly. Add "t" for et-words ("et koldt værelse") and "-e" for more than one. When you tell someone you feel cold you say "Jeg fryser" (I am freezing), not "jeg er kold", which would sound as though you are an unfriendly person.

sentence.en: It is too cold today.

forms.da: Kom nu, vi skal af sted.
forms.en: Come on, we have to go.

kom nu.explanation: "Kom nu" literally means "come now" and works like "come on". It can be encouraging, impatient or a little disbelieving, depending on your tone. Use it to hurry someone up or to say "oh, really?". It works the same with one person or many.

sentence.en: Come on, the bus leaves soon!

kontant.explanation: "Kontant" means in cash, as in real coins and notes. You use it with paying: "Jeg betaler kontant" (I pay in cash). Most Danish shops prefer cards, and some do not take cash at all, so "Tager I kontanter?" (Do you take cash?) is a useful question. The word does not change, whatever it describes.

sentence.en: I would like to pay in cash.

kort.explanation: "Kort" means short, for length or time, and it also works for a distance. With an et-word it keeps the same form (kort, not kort-t), and with many things or after "the" it takes "-e" (korte). It is also a thing-word: "et kort" means a card or a map. The opposite of the adjective is "lang".

sentence.en: I have a short break.

kulde.explanation: "Kulde" is the word for cold as a thing, as in cold weather or the feeling of cold. It is an en-word, so "the cold" is "kulden". Do not mix it up with "kold", which you use to describe something that is cold ("koldt vand"). The opposite is "varme".

sentence.da: Jeg er ikke vant til **kulden** her.
sentence.en: I am not used to the cold here.

kun.explanation: "Kun" means "only" or "just", and it limits whatever word comes after it. "Kun jeg ved det" means only I know it, while "Jeg ved kun det" means that is all I know. In everyday speech Danes also say "bare" for the same idea, but "kun" works everywhere.

sentence.en: I only have two hours.

kvart.explanation: "Kvart" means a quarter, and it is used in telling time. "Kvart over tre" is a quarter past three, and "kvart i fire" is a quarter to four. The same word is also used in "et kvarter" (a quarter of an hour, 15 minutes), so it is a useful word to know.

sentence.en: See you at a quarter past three.

kvart i.explanation: Means "quarter to". The hour that follows is the one coming up: "kvart i tre" is 2:45, fifteen minutes before three. Do not mix it up with "kvart over" (quarter past). A tip: "i" here works like "to" in "quarter to".

sentence.en: The film starts at quarter to seven.

kvart over.explanation: Means "quarter past". Put the hour after it: "kvart over tre" is 3:15. A quarter is "en kvart", and "over" means "past". Compare "kvart i" (quarter to), where the hour that follows is the next hour.

sentence.en: The bus comes at quarter past eight.

kvindelig.explanation: "Kvindelig" means female or feminine, and you use it to describe people or things connected to women. It is built from "kvinde" (woman). It is used on forms and in descriptions. The opposite is "mandlig".

sentence.en: My doctor is female.

kylling.explanation: "Kylling" is chicken, both the bird and the meat you eat. It is an en-word, so "the chicken" is "kyllingen". The plural "kyllinger" is used for the birds. For the meat you simply say "kylling" with no "a".

sentence.en: We are eating chicken for dinner.

kærlighed.explanation: "Kærlighed" means love, and it is an en-word, so "the love" is "kærligheden". It is usually used without "en" in front, as in "Kærlighed er vigtigt". It is the big, general word. For saying "I love you" you use the verb: "Jeg elsker dig". A loved one is "en kæreste".

sentence.en: Love is the most important thing in life.

kød.explanation: "Kød" means meat. It is an et-word, so "the meat" is "kødet". It is used for all kinds of meat as a group. To say what kind, you add a word in front, as in "oksekød" (beef) or "svinekød" (pork). People who do not eat meat are "vegetarer".

sentence.en: I do not eat much meat.

køn.explanation: "Køn" means pretty, usually about a person, a face or a place. With et-words it gets a "t" ("et kønt hus") and with more than one "ne" ("kønne piger"). Do not mix it up with "et køn", which means gender (male or female).

sentence.en: It is a pretty house.
